nodes.label: Quantum mechanics
nodes.definition: Fundamental physical theory of matter and light at quantum scales.
nodes.scope: Atomic, subatomic, molecular, optical, condensed-matter and information contexts, with extensions into QFT and quantum-gravity research.
nodes.epistemic_status: Experimentally highly successful; interpretation and quantum-gravity questions remain open.

nodes.label: Quantum state
nodes.definition: Normalized vector/ray in the complex Hilbert-space formulation.

nodes.label: Observable
nodes.definition: Self-adjoint/Hermitian linear operator representing a measurable physical quantity.
nodes.measurement_role: Its spectral structure determines possible outcomes and Born-rule probabilities.

nodes.label: Measurement
nodes.definition: Process that produces an outcome and, in the source's formulation, triggers a postulated state update.

nodes.label: Quantum decoherence
nodes.definition: Environment-induced entanglement that suppresses coherent quantum interference.

nodes.label: Quantum entanglement
nodes.definition: Nonseparability of a composite quantum state.

nodes.definition: σXσP≥ℏ/2 arising from canonical noncommutation of X and P.

nodes.label: QM is the fundamental physical theory describing matter and light, especially at atomic/subatomic scales.
Classical mechanics is an approximation to quantum mechanics at ordinary scales.
Bound quantum systems have discrete energy, momentum, angular momentum and other quantities.
Quantum measurements show both wave-like and particle-like characteristics.
The Born rule obtains probability from the squared absolute value of a complex probability amplitude.
Double-slit experiments produce interference in detection density while individual detections remain discrete.
Quantum tunnelling permits crossing a potential barrier below the classical kinetic-energy threshold.
Entanglement makes the joint system nonseparable from the perspective of individual component state vectors.
Bell tests violate constraints imposed by local hidden-variable theories.
A quantum state is a normalized vector in a separable complex Hilbert space, defined up to global phase.
Observables are self-adjoint/Hermitian linear operators; eigenstates/eigenvalues structure measurement outcomes.
The source presents a postulated state collapse/update after measurement and identifies it as foundationally debated.
The Schrödinger equation gives quantum time evolution using the Hamiltonian.
Hamiltonian eigenstates can have time-independent probability distributions and definite energies/frequencies.
Only a few simple systems are analytically solvable; perturbation theory provides approximate solutions.
Position and momentum obey [X,P]=iℏ and σXσP≥ℏ/2; a general commutator bound applies.
Position and momentum representations are Fourier transforms; p becomes -iℏ∂/∂x in position space.
Composite systems use tensor-product Hilbert spaces.
Superpositions of product states can be nonseparable; subsystem states require reduced density matrices.
Environment interaction entangles a system with its environment, producing decoherence.
Matrix mechanics, wave mechanics, transformation theory and path integrals are alternative/equivalent formulations.
Observables commuting with the Hamiltonian are conserved; differentiable symmetries correspond to conservation laws.
A one-dimensional free particle has H=P²/(2m) and is represented as a superposition of momentum eigenstates.
A Gaussian free-particle packet illustrates the uncertainty tradeoff and spreads in position during evolution.
An infinite potential well imposes boundary conditions that quantize k and energy.
Finite wells have nonzero wavefunctions outside the well; rectangular barriers model tunnelling.
The quantum harmonic oscillator has V=½mω²x² and E_n=ℏω(n+½).
The Mach–Zehnder interferometer models superposition/interference in a two-dimensional complex state space.
Quantum mechanics underlies quantum chemistry, optics, computing, semiconductors, lasers, imaging and more.
Relativistic particle creation/annihilation motivates quantum field theory; QED describes electromagnetism.
QCD is the quantum field theory of quarks and gluons; electroweak theory unifies weak and electromagnetic forces.
Quantum mechanics and general relativity remain difficult to reconcile; quantum gravity is an open problem.
String theory replaces point particles with strings; a vibrational state corresponds to a graviton.
Loop quantum gravity describes quantum spacetime with spin networks and spin foams at the Planck scale.
Interpretive debates concern probability, collapse, measurement and nonlocality; no consensus exists.
Copenhagen-type views emphasize probability and the dependence of well-defined applications on experimental arrangement.
EPR argued for incompleteness under locality assumptions; Bell later derived testable constraints.
Bohmian mechanics is deterministic and explicitly nonlocal, with real particle positions and a guiding equation.
Many-worlds removes collapse and retains all branches in a larger quantum superposition.
Quantum mechanics emerged through Planck, Einstein, Bohr, de Broglie, Heisenberg, Schrödinger, Born, Dirac and others.
Planck's 1900 quantum hypothesis introduced E=hν in solving black-body radiation.
Einstein used quanta to explain the photoelectric effect and later developed quantum radiation/stimulated emission.
De Broglie proposed matter waves in 1923.
Matrix and wave mechanics were developed in the mid-1920s; Born supplied probabilistic interpretation.

overview.statement: QM is the fundamental physical theory describing matter and light, especially at atomic/subatomic scales.

classical.statement: Classical mechanics is an approximation to quantum mechanics at ordinary scales.

quantization.statement: Bound quantum systems have discrete energy, momentum, angular momentum and other quantities.

duality.statement: Quantum measurements show both wave-like and particle-like characteristics.

born.statement: The Born rule obtains probability from the squared absolute value of a complex probability amplitude.

double_slit.statement: Double-slit experiments produce interference in detection density while individual detections remain discrete.

tunnel.statement: Quantum tunnelling permits crossing a potential barrier below the classical kinetic-energy threshold.

entangle.statement: Entanglement makes the joint system nonseparable from the perspective of individual component state vectors.

bell.statement: Bell tests violate constraints imposed by local hidden-variable theories.

hilbert.statement: A quantum state is a normalized vector in a separable complex Hilbert space, defined up to global phase.

observable.statement: Observables are self-adjoint/Hermitian linear operators; eigenstates/eigenvalues structure measurement outcomes.

collapse.statement: The source presents a postulated state collapse/update after measurement and identifies it as foundationally debated.

schrodinger.statement: The Schrödinger equation gives quantum time evolution using the Hamiltonian.

stationary.statement: Hamiltonian eigenstates can have time-independent probability distributions and definite energies/frequencies.

approx.statement: Only a few simple systems are analytically solvable; perturbation theory provides approximate solutions.

uncertainty.statement: Position and momentum obey [X,P]=iℏ and σXσP≥ℏ/2; a general commutator bound applies.

fourier.statement: Position and momentum representations are Fourier transforms; p becomes -iℏ∂/∂x in position space.

tensor.statement: Composite systems use tensor-product Hilbert spaces.

entangled_state.statement: Superpositions of product states can be nonseparable; subsystem states require reduced density matrices.

decoherence.statement: Environment interaction entangles a system with its environment, producing decoherence.

formulations.statement: Matrix mechanics, wave mechanics, transformation theory and path integrals are alternative/equivalent formulations.

symmetry.statement: Observables commuting with the Hamiltonian are conserved; differentiable symmetries correspond to conservation laws.

free.statement: A one-dimensional free particle has H=P²/(2m) and is represented as a superposition of momentum eigenstates.

gaussian.statement: A Gaussian free-particle packet illustrates the uncertainty tradeoff and spreads in position during evolution.

box.statement: An infinite potential well imposes boundary conditions that quantize k and energy.

finite_well.statement: Finite wells have nonzero wavefunctions outside the well; rectangular barriers model tunnelling.

oscillator.statement: The quantum harmonic oscillator has V=½mω²x² and E_n=ℏω(n+½).

mzi.statement: The Mach–Zehnder interferometer models superposition/interference in a two-dimensional complex state space.

apps.statement: Quantum mechanics underlies quantum chemistry, optics, computing, semiconductors, lasers, imaging and more.

qft.statement: Relativistic particle creation/annihilation motivates quantum field theory; QED describes electromagnetism.

qcd.statement: QCD is the quantum field theory of quarks and gluons; electroweak theory unifies weak and electromagnetic forces.

qgravity.statement: Quantum mechanics and general relativity remain difficult to reconcile; quantum gravity is an open problem.

string.statement: String theory replaces point particles with strings; a vibrational state corresponds to a graviton.

lqg.statement: Loop quantum gravity describes quantum spacetime with spin networks and spin foams at the Planck scale.

interpretations.statement: Interpretive debates concern probability, collapse, measurement and nonlocality; no consensus exists.

copenhagen.statement: Copenhagen-type views emphasize probability and the dependence of well-defined applications on experimental arrangement.

epr.statement: EPR argued for incompleteness under locality assumptions; Bell later derived testable constraints.

bohm.statement: Bohmian mechanics is deterministic and explicitly nonlocal, with real particle positions and a guiding equation.

manyworlds.statement: Many-worlds removes collapse and retains all branches in a larger quantum superposition.

history.statement: Quantum mechanics emerged through Planck, Einstein, Bohr, de Broglie, Heisenberg, Schrödinger, Born, Dirac and others.

planck.statement: Planck's 1900 quantum hypothesis introduced E=hν in solving black-body radiation.

einstein.statement: Einstein used quanta to explain the photoelectric effect and later developed quantum radiation/stimulated emission.

debroglie.statement: De Broglie proposed matter waves in 1923.

modern.statement: Matrix and wave mechanics were developed in the mid-1920s; Born supplied probabilistic interpretation.

semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: A wave function is a representation; the rigorous state is a Hilbert-space ray.
Complex amplitudes interfere; probabilities are obtained after modulus-square.
The operator defines possible spectral outcomes; measurement returns an outcome.
The source distinguishes deterministic unitary evolution from postulated collapse.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Quantum uncertainty vs ordinary measurement error
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: The formal bound arises from operator noncommutation.
Entangled states cannot be written as one tensor product.
Environment-induced decoherence is not simply identical to a fundamental collapse postulate.
Classical mechanics is treated as a limiting approximation.
Equivalent mathematical formulations can share different interpretive positions.
Bell constrains local hidden-variable combinations; Bohmian mechanics retains determinism while giving up locality.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Quantum mechanics vs quantum field theory
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: QFT is needed when relativistic field effects and particle creation/annihilation matter.
Both are empirically successful but difficult to combine formally.

historical_timeline.event: Thomas Young describes the double-slit experiment.
Gustav Kirchhoff identifies the black-body radiation problem.
Planck introduces the quantum hypothesis for black-body radiation.
Einstein applies the quantum hypothesis to the photoelectric effect.
Einstein's quantum radiation work articulates stimulated emission.
Born introduces the probabilistic interpretation of the wave function.
Hilbert, Dirac and von Neumann further formalize quantum mechanics.
The EPR argument challenges completeness under locality assumptions.

Expand pure/mixed states, partial trace, purification, entropy and open-system states.

Add Coulomb Hamiltonian, quantum numbers, orbitals, degeneracy, spectra and selection rules.
Add identical particles, exchange symmetry, bosons, fermions, Fock space and correlations.
Add asymptotic states, S-matrix, cross sections, phase shifts and Born approximation.
Connect decoherence to master equations, Lindblad dynamics and environment-induced superselection.
Add qubits, gates, channels, entropy, teleportation, error correction and cryptography.
Expand Bell, contextuality, hidden variables, operational reconstructions and interpretations.
Add band structure, Fermi statistics, superconductivity, superfluidity and topological phases.
Expand gauge symmetry, fields, quantization, renormalization and particle creation.
